WORRY GUIDE — LIFE

When you're torn over apologizing

A remark you went too far with, a message you couldn't reply to, a promise that slipped past each other. You know you should apologize, yet the more you miss the moment, the harder it becomes to bring up. When you picture the other person's face, excuses come to mind first. The longer being torn over whether to apologize drags on, the heavier it makes the relationship itself. To be clear at the outset, apologizing is not losing. It is your own choice about what you want for the relationship. This page guides you through how to take that step.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

There are broadly three reasons you can't apologize and feel torn. One is resistance to admitting your own fault. When the extreme equation that apologizing means everything is your fault sits in your head, you can't take the step. The second is fear of the other person's reaction. Will they be angry? Will they not forgive you? Fear of a reaction that hasn't happened yet becomes the reason to put it off. The third is awkwardness about having missed the timing itself. The more time passes, the bigger the feeling of 'after all this time' grows, and on top of apologizing you end up carrying the delay as well. Once you can see what's making this hard, what you need to think about next shifts from whether to apologize to what you want for this relationship.

POINT 02

How to sort it out

First, write the facts out in three parts: what happened to the other person, what you did or didn't do, and what you want from here. What an apology needs is mainly the second and third. Excuses tend to slip into the first, so leave them out deliberately. Next, decide the scope of the apology. You don't need to take on everything; the range of your own words and actions is enough. Once the scope is set, you can keep the wording short. This writing goes more easily if you do it while drawing a card and looking at it. The card is not there to tell you to apologize; it is a mirror reflecting your current state — fear, stubbornness, or regret. If you keep a record in a log of when you apologized and when you let it go, it becomes material for not repeating the same mismatch.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

When you're torn over whether to apologize, cards that speak to adjustment, regret, a turning point, moving forward, and choosing again can offer useful clues.

Temperance shows an angel pouring water between two cups. It offers a perspective for balancing emotion and fact, and finding just the right way to convey it.

The Five of Cups is a figure gazing at toppled cups. Your eyes tend to go to what was lost, but behind the figure there are cups still standing and a bridge.

Judgement shows people waking at the sound of a trumpet. It points to a chance to draw a line under the past and begin the relationship again.

The Six of Swords shows a boat crossing calm water. It represents moving away from the place of conflict toward a calmer place.

The Lovers shows two people facing each other. It points to the importance of choosing again, including whether to continue the relationship.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions. Of what happened to the other person, what weighed heaviest? Which part of your own words and actions would you want to take back? In one sentence, what is the scope of your apology? After apologizing, what do you want for this relationship? If you leave it without apologizing, how are your feelings likely to change? Once your answers are together, all that is left is to convey it. Briefly — the facts, your feelings, and what comes next. Apologizing is not work that digs the past back up; it is an act that decides what comes next in the relationship.

FAQ

Frequently asked questions

When is a good time to apologize?

When the other person's emotions have settled a little and you have a setting where the two of you can talk. An apology right in the heat of the moment can add fuel to the fire, and one that is too late is treated as if nothing happened. As a guide, within the same day or by the next day. A stance of listening to the other person first reaches them before your words do.

Should I apologize even when I don't think I was in the wrong?

An apology for the facts and an apology for having hurt the other person are different things. Even if you were not at fault, you can touch on the fact that they had an unpleasant experience. You don't need to admit to everything. An apology with a line drawn is not giving in; it is a skill for protecting the relationship.

What matters most when apologizing?

Not mixing in excuses. The moment a 'but' or 'because' enters, an apology turns into a justification. Put into concrete words what was wrong, and add one thing about what you will do from next time. Those two are enough; a long letter of apology is not needed.

Apologize, or watch how things go? Why not separate the facts from your feelings, and think about what comes next in the relationship?
